questions.text: Why allocate a shared visual-token budget differently across single-image, multi-image, and video inputs?

options.A: To make every scenario use identical image resolution and frame counts.
options.B: To eliminate the need for image encoders when processing video inputs.
options.C: To guarantee that temporal reasoning improves whenever tokens are removed.
options.D: To balance spatial detail against image or frame coverage within bounded context.

questions.explanation: Single images can spend tokens on detail; multi-image and video inputs distribute the budget over more views or frames, often using spatial pooling.

questions.text: A video has 32 sampled frames, each with a 24×24 patch grid. Pooling each grid to 8×8 gives how many visual tokens in total?
questions.explanation: Each pooled frame has 8×8=64 tokens; 32 frames produce 32×64=2048 tokens.

questions.text: After every candidate exceeds the budget, plan_video returns {"n_frames": 8, "per_frame": 64, "total": 512}. What happens for budget=100?

options.A: It raises an exception because no candidate fits the budget.
options.B: It reduces the frame count until total tokens are at most 100.
options.C: It returns the fallback even though its 512 tokens exceed the budget.
options.D: It returns an empty plan with zero frames and zero tokens.

questions.explanation: The fallback is returned unconditionally after the loops. There is no final budget check, so the planner does not enforce its advertised limit for very small budgets.
